definition: A fiduciary relationship in which an agent acts on a principal’s behalf and subject to the principal’s control, with mutual assent.
The person for whom an agent acts.
A person authorized to act for another within an agency relationship.
Authority based on the agent’s reasonable understanding of the principal’s manifestations to the agent.
Power arising from a third party’s reasonable belief traceable to the principal’s manifestations.
A principal’s later affirmance of an act, giving it effect as if originally authorized when the legal requirements are met.
An employer’s vicarious liability for an employee’s tort within the scope of employment.
An obligation arising from a relationship of trust, including applicable duties of loyalty and care.
A duty to protect the beneficiary’s interests against prohibited self-dealing, competition, or appropriation of opportunities.
The applicable standard of diligence and conduct; the precise rule depends on the relationship and governing law.
An association of two or more persons carrying on as co-owners a business for profit, whether or not they intend the legal label.
Liability under which a claimant may, subject to applicable rules, collect the entire obligation from any liable partner.
A partner’s departure from the association; it does not invariably require dissolution.
The event that starts winding up a partnership when the governing rules require it.
Completing the business’s unfinished affairs, settling liabilities, and distributing remaining assets.
Protection against personal liability solely because of ownership status; it does not excuse one’s own wrongful conduct.
A limited liability company: a statutory entity whose governance depends on applicable law and its operating agreement.
An LLC’s governing agreement, subject to the mandatory limits of the applicable statute.
An LLC structure in which members generally exercise management authority under the governing law and agreement.
An LLC structure assigning management to designated managers rather than automatically to every member.
The corporation’s public formation document, sometimes called its certificate or charter.
Internal corporate governance rules subordinate to controlling law and the charter.
The body generally charged with managing or directing the corporation’s business and affairs.
An owner of corporate shares; ownership does not itself grant authority to act as the corporation’s agent.
A presumption protecting qualifying informed, disinterested, good-faith board decisions from judicial second-guessing.
A business opportunity that fiduciary law may require a fiduciary to present to the entity rather than take personally.
A suit by an owner on the entity’s behalf to redress an injury to the entity, subject to procedural requirements.
An exceptional basis for disregarding entity separateness and imposing owner liability under the jurisdiction’s test.
Mixing entity and personal funds or assets, which can undermine evidence of genuine separateness.
A person who helps organize a corporation and may incur personal obligations on pre-incorporation contracts.
Crediting profit or charging loss to an owner’s economic account; it need not involve a current cash payment.
A transfer of money or property from an entity to an owner in the owner’s capacity as owner, subject to the agreement and statutory limits.
A person treated as an owner based on the actual control and ownership relationship despite lacking formal share title; wrongful use remains a separate veil piercing requirement.
Equity shares carrying the rights specified by the charter and statute, commonly including residual economic and voting rights.
An equity class or series with specified preferences or special rights; examine the charter rather than assuming a universal bundle.
An instrument representing a creditor claim, rather than an equity ownership interest.
An agreement substituting a new obligation or obligor and releasing the old obligation or obligor; corporate adoption alone does not necessarily release a promoter.
A traditional doctrine recognizing certain good faith incorporation attempts with actual corporate use, where the governing jurisdiction permits it.
A doctrine that can prevent a party who dealt with a business as a corporation from denying its corporate status in the relevant dispute; its availability and effects vary.
A permitted limitation on specified liability, such as certain monetary fiduciary liability under a charter provision; it differs from eliminating duties or providing indemnification.
A cost or benefit borne outside the decision maker’s transaction, such as uncompensated harm where corporate assets cannot satisfy a claim.
A risk characteristic of the employer’s enterprise; Bushey used this concept in its historical scope of employment analysis.
